title: File:Broken glass bottles hazardous waste in dispersed quantities ecotoxicological question 01.JPG
description:
Example of hazardous waste in dispersed quantities.
Broken glass (here, it is a bottle of beer crushed by a bus, on an urban road in front of a bus shelter).
Questions for ecotoxicology: What happens to these tiny pieces of glass very sharp when they are washed away by rain into rivers? What becomes after being carried by the wind? They are dangerous? and how long? when they come in tons of dust collected by municipal sweepers. Many fragments are carried away by sewers to the treatment plant or grease recovery systems and gravel .. Where are they now? They may sewage sludge containing crushed or broken glass be spread on agricultural fields? What will happen when a worm ingests such fragments, and a pheasant eat what earthworms, etc. .
categories: Broken glass bottles|Self-published work

title: File:Broken glass bottles hazardous waste in dispersed quantities ecotoxicological question 08.jpg
description:
Example of hazardous waste in dispersed quantity.

Broken glass (here it is a green vine bottle crushed by cars, on an urban road, in Lille (northern France).

Questions for the ecotoxicologist : What happens to these tiny pieces of very sharp glass when they are carried away by the rain to the streams? What happens after they have been carried away by the wind? Are they still dangerous? And how long ? when they are (by tons) collected in dust harvested by the municipal sweepers. Many fragments are carried by sewers to sewage treatment plants or grease and gravel recovery systems. What happens to them? Will sewage sludge containing crushed or broken glass be spread on cultivated fields? What happens when an earthworm ingests such fragments, and a pheasant eats this earthworm, etc. .

title: File:Open refrigerator with food at night.jpg
description:
An open domestic refrigerator with food and drink at night.
The photo is stacked for focus and light from five photos.
The only light source used is the normal lamp in the fridge.
The fridge in an Electrolux, model ERB34253W with a net volume of 188 litres (6.6 cu ft).
The fridge contains four eggs, a green bell pepper, a jar of chili, three bottles of grapefruit soda, three cans of coconut milk, three bottles of pear cider, a bottle of carbonated water, a bottle of soy sauce, a plate of sliced ham, a container with butter, a round cheese, a jar of sliced, pickled cucumber, a pitcher with crushed, roasted cacao beans, two lemons, some tomatoes, a box with grapes, carrots, yellow onions and oranges. The fridge is in Brastad, Lysekil Municipality, Sweden.

title: File:Pomegranate Fruit Nectar Juice with ice cubes.jpg
attribution: TAPAS KUMAR HALDER
description: You can press the seeds from a pomegranate into juice. A large pomegranate will yield between 1/4 and 1/2 cup of juice.To extract the juice, crush the seeds in a food mill or sieve. You can also blend the seeds, then pour the liquefied mixture through a strainer to remove any leftover pulp from the juice.You can freeze or can pomegranate juice to make it last longer. If you choose to can it, add a few tablespoons of lemon juice to it before sealing the can to maintain the juice's vibrant color.

title: File:Medieval bell (FindID 938436).jpg
attribution: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Helena Costas, 2019-10-08 10:06:40
credit:
https://finds.org.uk/database/ajax/download/id/1075938
Catalog: https://finds.org.uk/database/images/image/id/1075938/recordtype/artefacts archive copy at the Wayback Machine
Artefact: https://finds.org.uk/database/artefacts/record/id/938436
description:
Description: An incomplete bell possibly dating to the medieval period. The bell is lozenge-shaped in plan and has four petal-like tabs. The bell has been flattened to the point where two of the petals have joined with the opposing two petals. There is also a circular concave dent on the upper part of both sides of the bell. The top of the bell has an oval suspension loop attached which is 5.4mm in height. The loop is slightly bent back. The bell consists of a semi-spherical upper half which is moulded to the lower four petals. It is uncertain if the pea remains inside the bell. The upper half of the bell is decorated with two strips which descend from the base of the suspension loop down to the moulded joint of the two halves. The left strip takes the form of a feather-like design, and the right strip comprises cross-hatched lines descending parallel to each other. The design is repeated on the other side of the bell. The petals of the bell are decorated with cross-hatching which covers the entire surfaces.

Scientific analysis: Analysis was carried out by Department of Scientific Research at the British Museum. Non-destructive X-ray fluorescence analysis of the surface the bell indicated a likely metal content of more than 98% tin, with traces of lead and copper.

Dimensions:

Length: 28.1 mm

Width: 21 mm

Thickness: 8.8 mm

Weight: 4.34 g

Discussion: Similar examples have been recorded on the PAS database. For examples see: YORYM-E51788, YORYM-747851, SWYOR-F92A53, and SUR-476322. Similar examples can also be found in (Egan and Pritchard 2002, page 339, nos. 1668 and 1679). These were all made from tin, and found in contexts of ceramic phase 7 (c. 1200-c. 1230).

Conclusion: The bell is more than 300 years old, but is not 10% silver, so does not qualify as Treasure under the stipulations of the Treasure Act 1996.

title: File:Toothbrush regurgitated by albatross on Tern Island, Hawaii - 20060614.jpg
credit: United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), Hawaiian Islands NWR.
description: An albatross bolus – undigested matter from the diet such as squid beaks and fish scales. This bolus from a Hawaiian albatross (either a Black-footed Albatross or a Laysan Albatross) found on Tern Island, in the French Frigate Shoals, Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, has several ingested flotsam items, including monofilament fishing line from fishing nets and a discarded toothbrush. Ingestion of plastic flotsam is an increasing hazard for albatrosses.
